pairs.question: I heard that a lot of adults smoke. Is that true?
pairs.answer: Yes, in the United States, 1 in 5 adults uses tobacco products. It's a significant public health issue.
pairs.evidence: In the United States, 1 in 5 adults uses tobacco products.

pairs.question: What’s the main reason smoking is a big deal?
pairs.answer: Cigarette smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease and death in the United States. It's really important to take it seriously.
pairs.evidence: Cigarette smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease and death in the United States despite its known health effects.

pairs.question: I want to quit smoking, but I’m worried I won’t be able to do it.
pairs.answer: You're not alone! Although nearly one-half of people who smoke try to quit each year, only up to 1 in 20 who quit without support achieve abstinence for at least six months.
pairs.evidence: Although nearly one-half of people who smoke try to quit each year, only up to 1 in 20 who quit without support achieve abstinence for at least six months.

pairs.question: Should I talk to my kids about smoking?
pairs.answer: Absolutely! All patients, including school-aged children and adolescents, should be asked if they smoke and offered evidence-based treatments for smoking cessation.
pairs.evidence: All patients, including school-aged children and adolescents, should be asked if they smoke and offered evidence-based treatments for smoking cessation.

pairs.question: What’s the 5 A’s framework for quitting smoking?
pairs.answer: The 5 A’s framework includes ask, advise, assess, assist, and arrange. It can really help in promoting smoking cessation.
pairs.evidence: Use of the 5 A’s framework (ask, advise, assess, assist, arrange) can help clinicians promote smoking cessation.

pairs.question: Is it better to use medication or just go cold turkey?
pairs.answer: Combining pharmacotherapy with effective behavior strategies is significantly more effective than either approach alone. So, using both can really help!
pairs.evidence: Clinical studies have demonstrated that combining pharmacotherapy with effective behavior strategies is significantly more effective than either approach alone.

pairs.question: What medications can help me quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Pharmacotherapies approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for smoking cessation include nicotine replacement therapy, bupropion, and varenicline. It's great that you're looking for options to help you quit!
pairs.evidence: Pharmacotherapies approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for smoking cessation include nicotine replacement therapy, bupropion, and varenicline.

pairs.question: How long should I use smoking cessation medications?
pairs.answer: Extended use (greater than 12 weeks) of a controller therapy (varenicline, bupropion, or nicotine patch) is associated with significantly higher sustained quit rates and lower relapse rates than standard use (six to 12 weeks). This could really boost your chances of quitting!
pairs.evidence: Extended use (greater than 12 weeks) of a controller therapy (varenicline, bupropion, or nicotine patch) is associated with significantly higher sustained quit rates and lower relapse rates than standard use (six to 12 weeks).

pairs.question: Are e-cigarettes a good option for quitting smoking?
pairs.answer: e-Cigarettes are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for smoking cessation, and evidence supporting their benefit is inconclusive. It's important to consider other options that are proven to work.
pairs.evidence: e-Cigarettes are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for smoking cessation, and evidence supporting their benefit is inconclusive.

pairs.question: Who should get lung cancer screening?
pairs.answer: Lung cancer screening is recommended for adults 50 to 80 years of age who have a 20-pack-year smoking history and currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years. It's a good idea to stay on top of your health!
pairs.evidence: Lung cancer screening is recommended for adults 50 to 80 years of age who have a 20-pack-year smoking history and currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years.

pairs.question: How common is tobacco use in the U.S.?
pairs.answer: In the United States, 1 in 5 adults uses tobacco products. It's more common than many people realize, but you can be part of the change!
pairs.evidence: In the United States, 1 in 5 adults uses tobacco products.

pairs.question: What percentage of tobacco use comes from cigarettes?
pairs.answer: Cigarettes and other forms of combustible tobacco products (cigars and pipes) account for 80.5% of tobacco use. Knowing this can help you understand the impact of quitting.
pairs.evidence: Cigarettes and other forms of combustible tobacco products (cigars and pipes) account for 80.5% of tobacco use.

pairs.question: Why should I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Despite the known health effects of cigarettes, smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease and death in the United States. Quitting can significantly improve your health!
pairs.evidence: Despite the known health effects of cigarettes, smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease and death in the United States.

pairs.question: What should I do if I smoke?
pairs.answer: All nonpregnant adults who smoke cigarettes should be offered pharmacotherapy and behavior interventions to help cessation attempts. You're not alone in this journey!
pairs.evidence: All nonpregnant adults who smoke cigarettes should be offered pharmacotherapy and behavior interventions to help cessation attempts.

pairs.question: What can help me quit smoking?
pairs.answer: You can be offered pharmacotherapy and behavior interventions to help with your cessation attempts. Combining these methods can improve your chances of quitting.
pairs.evidence: be offered pharmacotherapy and behavior interventions to help cessation attempts.

pairs.question: Are combined interventions really more effective?
pairs.answer: Yes, behavior interventions combined with pharmacotherapy improve smoking cessation rates. They are more effective than usual care or minimal intervention.
pairs.evidence: Behavior interventions combined with pharmacotherapy improve smoking cessation rates.

pairs.question: What should pregnant people do about smoking?
pairs.answer: All pregnant people should be screened for tobacco use and advised to quit. They should also receive behavior interventions to help with cessation.
pairs.evidence: All pregnant people should be screened for tobacco use, advised to quit, and provided behavior interventions to help with cessation.

pairs.question: What should we do about kids and smoking?
pairs.answer: School-aged children and adolescents younger than 18 years should be asked about tobacco and e-cigarette use. They should receive interventions to prevent initiation of tobacco use.
pairs.evidence: School-aged children and adolescents younger than 18 years should be asked about tobacco and e-cigarette use and provided with interventions to prevent initiation of tobacco use.

pairs.question: Can kids get help to quit smoking?
pairs.answer: There is insufficient evidence to recommend behavior interventions or pharmacotherapy to help cessation efforts in children and adolescents. Prevention is the focus for this age group.
pairs.evidence: There is insufficient evidence to recommend behavior interventions or pharmacotherapy to help cessation efforts in this population.

pairs.question: I heard that many people try to quit smoking every year. Is that true?
pairs.answer: Yes, almost one-half of people who smoke try to quit each year. It's a common effort, but it can be tough without support.
pairs.evidence: Almost one-half of people who smoke try to quit each year; however, only up to 1 in 20 of those who quit without support achieve abstinence for at least six months.

pairs.question: What are my chances of quitting if I go it alone?
pairs.answer: If you try to quit without support, only up to 1 in 20 will achieve abstinence for at least six months. It's really challenging to do it alone.
pairs.evidence: Almost one-half of people who smoke try to quit each year; however, only up to 1 in 20 of those who quit without support achieve abstinence for at least six months.

pairs.question: Can talking to my doctor help me quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Yes! Brief discussions with clinicians can increase cessation rates by two-thirds. Even a little support can make a big difference.
pairs.evidence: Brief discussions with clinicians can increase cessation rates by two-thirds, and more intensive treatment doubles the chances of quitting.

pairs.question: What if my doctor just asks about my smoking status?
pairs.answer: Including smoking status with the vital sign assessment has not resulted in increased smoking cessation rates. It's important for clinicians to address smoking more often.
pairs.evidence: Including smoking status with the vital sign assessment has not resulted in increased smoking cessation rates.

pairs.question: Does training help doctors support quitting?
pairs.answer: Absolutely! Studies show that clinicians who are trained in smoking cessation and knowledgeable about local resources are more likely to provide interventions.
pairs.evidence: Studies have shown that clinicians who are trained in smoking cessation and knowledgeable about local resources are more likely to provide smoking cessation interventions.

pairs.question: What does RCT mean in smoking cessation studies?
pairs.answer: RCT stands for randomized controlled trial. It's a type of study that helps determine the effectiveness of interventions.
pairs.evidence: RCT = randomized controlled trial; USPSTF = U.S. Preventive Services Task Force.

pairs.question: Why is it important for clinicians to be trained in smoking cessation?
pairs.answer: Clinicians who are trained in smoking cessation and knowledgeable about local resources are more likely to provide smoking cessation interventions. It's crucial for effective support in quitting smoking.
pairs.evidence: at clinicians who are trained in smoking cessation and knowledgeable about local resources are more likely to provide smoking cessation interventions.

pairs.question: Should I be asked about smoking even if I'm young?
pairs.answer: Yes, all patients should be asked if they smoke, regardless of age, sex, or medical history. More than one-half of adult smokers start smoking daily before 18 years of age.
pairs.evidence: All patients should be asked if they smoke, regardless of age, sex, or medical history. This includes school-aged children and adolescents because more than one-half of adult smokers start smoking daily before 18 years of age.

pairs.question: What if my doctor doesn't have time to talk about quitting smoking?
pairs.answer: If clinicians may not have adequate time, simplified models like AAR (ask, advise, refer to treatment resources) or AAC (ask, advise, connect patients to a quitline) can be used. There are options to help you even in busy settings.
pairs.evidence: Acknowledging that clinicians may not have adequate time and may not feel comfortable treating tobacco use disorders, simplified models such as AAR (ask, advise, refer to treatment resources) or AAC (ask, advise, connect patients to a quitline via fax, phone, or electronic referral) can be used.

pairs.question: Should I set a quit date right away?
pairs.answer: Attempts to set quit dates may be counterproductive because cessation rates increase steadily during pretreatment. Sometimes, focusing on readiness to quit is more beneficial.
pairs.evidence: Attempts to set quit dates may be counterproductive because cessation rates increase steadily during pretreatment.

pairs.question: Why is it beneficial to link smoking cessation codes to patient resources?
pairs.answer: Linking smoking cessation codes to patient resources provides access to local, up-to-date treatments and referrals. This can enhance the support available to those trying to quit.
pairs.evidence: In electronic health records, these codes can also be linked to patient resources or clinician tools for local, up-to-date treatments and referrals.
